claim: More in Common's April 2025 MRP poll (Reform 180 seats, Labour 165, Conservatives 165, Lib Dems 67) was explicitly caveated by its own publisher as not representing a projection of the eventual election result, given 4.5 years remained before the next mandatory general election.
stance_target: MRP polls conducted years before an election should be read as outcome projections
scope_conditions: UK, April 2025, MRP conducted years ahead of the statutory election date
quoted_support: With four and a half years before the next general election must be called this model is unlikely to represent anything close to the ultimate result and should not be seen as a projection of the election.

claim: MRP surveys typically achieve an average sample size of only about 25 respondents per constituency across Great Britain's 632 constituencies, relying on demographic priors from census/other sources to compensate for this sparse direct data.
stance_target: typical raw sample density underlying UK constituency-level MRP
scope_conditions: UK, contemporary MRP practice, 632 GB constituencies
quoted_support: Agencies ask a very large sample of electors about their voting intentions – enough to have an average sample size of about 25 respondents in each of the 632 constituencies in Great Britain.

claim: In practice, MRP's accuracy assumptions are not always met: a peer-reviewed Cambridge Political Analysis study found that the conditions required for MRP to perform well with conventional national surveys are 'not always met by practitioners.'
stance_target: MRP reliably meets its theoretical accuracy conditions in applied political-polling practice
scope_conditions: general MRP applied practice, conventional (non-massive) national survey samples
quoted_support: the conditions required for MRP to work well are not always met by practitioners.

claim: MRP's constituency-level demographic poststratification variables (notably social class) have lost most of their predictive power in Britain: the strong positive relationship between working-class share and Labour vote share at constituency level, clearly visible in 1964, had 'largely disappeared' by the 2019 general election.
stance_target: demographic covariates (esp. class) remain strong predictors of constituency vote share for MRP poststratification in contemporary Britain
scope_conditions: Britain, constituency-level analysis comparing 1964 and 2019 general elections
quoted_support: By then the relationship between the size of the working class and Labour voting at the constituency level had largely disappeared.

claim: More in Common's own regular (non-MRP) national poll outperformed its own MRP poll in predicting the actual result of the 2024 UK general election.
stance_target: MRP is systematically more accurate than conventional polling at forecasting an imminent election outcome
scope_conditions: UK, 2024 general election, single pollster (More in Common) same-house comparison
quoted_support: Just prior to polling day it conducted a regular poll alongside an MRP poll, and it turned out that the regular one was more accurate in predicting the result than the MRP poll.
